directAnswer: Pope Gregory VI, born John Gratian, was a respected Roman archpriest who became pope in May 1045 after paying Benedict IX to resign. Though welcomed by reformers, he was removed at the Council of Sutri in 1046 for simony and died in exile in Germany, accompanied by the future Pope Gregory VII.

sections.h2: John Gratian, Archpriest of St. John at the Latin Gate
paras: John Gratian was archpriest of the church of St. John at the Latin Gate in Rome and was Benedict IX's godfather. He was known for his piety and learning. When Benedict was willing to resign, John Gratian paid him a large sum to step aside and was installed as pope on 1 May 1045, taking the name Gregory.
Reform-minded churchmen were at first delighted. St. Peter Damian wrote to the new pope, welcoming him as a restorer of the Church's dignity after the turmoil of Benedict's reign.

sections.h2: A Reform-Minded Pope with a Tainted Title
paras: Gregory's motives appear to have been sincere: he seems to have wanted to free the Church from a pope widely seen as unworthy. But the payment was hard to distinguish from simony. As Benedict IX and Sylvester III continued to press their own claims, Rome had three rival popes, and Gregory was unable to secure control of the city or its revenues.

King Henry III of Germany came to Italy in 1046, intending to be crowned emperor and determined to end the confusion. He convened a council at Sutri on 20 December 1046. Gregory presided at first, but when the facts of his election were examined, he either resigned or was deposed; the sources give different accounts. A few days later Henry's candidate, Suidger of Bamberg, was elected as Clement II.

Sutri showed that a German king could settle a disputed papacy by his own authority. Reformers welcomed the result, which ended the scandal of rival claimants, but later generations grew uneasy with the precedent of royal control over who sat in the chair of Peter.

Gregory was sent into exile in Germany, where he died in 1047 or 1048, probably near Cologne. A young Roman cleric named Hildebrand, his chaplain, accompanied him. Hildebrand returned to Rome with Leo IX and later became pope himself in 1073. Many historians think his choice of the name Gregory VII was a tribute to his old patron, implying that he regarded Gregory VI as a legitimate pope.

keyFacts: Born John Gratian; archpriest of St. John at the Latin Gate
Godfather of Benedict IX, whom he paid to resign
Removed at the Council of Sutri under Henry III
Died in exile in Germany; accompanied by Hildebrand, the future Gregory VII

faqs.question: Why was Gregory VI removed?
faqs.answer: He had paid Benedict IX to resign. Though his motives may have been good, the Council of Sutri treated the payment as simony.

faqs.question: How is Gregory VI connected to Gregory VII?
faqs.answer: Hildebrand, later Gregory VII, served as his chaplain and followed him into exile. Many historians believe his papal name honored Gregory VI.

faqs.question: What did reformers think of Gregory VI?
faqs.answer: Many welcomed him at first. St. Peter Damian wrote to congratulate him, hoping he would restore order to the Church.
